summary: Goal pathways for the Good Dog app: one owner goal as ordered stages, each with a gate the dog passes before the next. Same shape as the UK Lite course weeks (gate, opensAfter, ifGateFails), scoped to one goal. Format: ixOS docs/good-dog-demo.md, "Pathway format".

pathways.title: Coming back when called
pathways.summary: From turning to their name to coming back on a long line with mild distractions.

stages.title: Turning to their name
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog looks your way when they hear their name, said once.
stages.whyItMatters: Every recall starts with your dog turning towards you. A name that always pays off is the first step of coming back.
stages.everydayPractice: Say their name once when they are already about to look at you, and reward the look.

gate.summary: Orients to you within 2 seconds of their name, said once at normal volume, in low distraction.
gate.ownerCheck: In a quiet room, does {dog} look at you within a couple of seconds of hearing their name once?

stages.ifGateFails: Shorten the game, go somewhere quieter and use a reward your dog loves. Say the name once, not again and again.
stages.maintenance: Reward a few name responses on ordinary days, especially when your dog chooses to look at you.

stages.title: Coming back nearby
stages.whatItMeans: One recall word, and your dog comes to you in a quiet, enclosed space or on a long line.
stages.whyItMatters: A recall that always pays off at home is the base for every place after it.
stages.everydayPractice: Call once when your dog is already heading your way, and make arriving worth it.

gate.summary: Returns to arm's reach on a 5 m long line, to a single cue, in low distraction.
gate.ownerCheck: On a 5 metre long line somewhere quiet, does {dog} come back to arm's reach when called once?

stages.ifGateFails: Go back to the name game and shorten the distance. Don't repeat the recall word if your dog is unlikely to come; go and get them calmly instead.
stages.maintenance: A few rewarded recalls on ordinary walks each week, and never call only to end the fun.

stages.title: Coming back with mild distractions
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog comes back on a longer line when there is something mildly interesting around.
stages.whyItMatters: Real walks have smells, people and other dogs. Practising with small distractions first builds a recall that holds up outside.
stages.everydayPractice: On a long line, call once when the distraction is still far away, and reward generously when your dog comes.

gate.summary: Reliable recall on a 10 m long line with mild distraction. This does not unlock off-lead freedom in public.
gate.ownerCheck: On a 10 metre long line with something mildly interesting nearby, does {dog} come back when called once?

stages.ifGateFails: Make the distraction smaller or further away, or go back to the quiet place for a few days. Keep the long line on.
stages.maintenance: Keep the long line for new places. Off-lead only in secure areas you know, or with a trainer's advice.

pathways.title: Walking nicely on the lead
pathways.summary: From being comfortable on the lead to checking in with you on walks.

stages.title: Comfortable on the lead
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog is relaxed while the lead goes on and walks a few steps beside you at home.
stages.whyItMatters: A dog who is comfortable wearing the lead can start to learn where the reward is.
stages.everydayPractice: Clip the lead on for a moment at home, reward, and take it off again.

gate.summary: Stays relaxed while the lead is clipped on and walks a few steps beside you indoors.
gate.ownerCheck: At home, does {dog} stay relaxed while you clip the lead on, and walk a few steps beside you?

stages.ifGateFails: Keep the sessions very short, check the harness fits comfortably, and reward just for the lead going on.
stages.maintenance: Make the lead going on a calm, good moment before every walk.

stages.title: A loose lead
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog walks beside you with the lead slack, starting somewhere quiet.
stages.whyItMatters: Pulling works when it gets your dog where they want to go. Stopping when the lead goes tight, and rewarding by your side, teaches that a loose lead is what gets them there.
stages.everydayPractice: On the first minutes of a walk, stop when the lead goes tight and move on when it's slack again.

gate.summary: Ten consecutive steps with a slack lead without you stopping.
gate.ownerCheck: Somewhere quiet, can {dog} walk ten steps in a row beside you with the lead slack?

stages.ifGateFails: Go back indoors or to the garden, reward more often at your side, and keep walks short and calm while you practise.
stages.maintenance: Reward walking at your side now and then on ordinary walks.

stages.title: Checking in on walks
stages.whatItMeans: On walks, your dog looks back at you from time to time without being asked.
stages.whyItMatters: A dog who checks in keeps the lead loose by choice and is easier to call when something comes up.
stages.everydayPractice: Carry a few treats and reward every time your dog looks back at you on a walk.

gate.summary: Checks in with you without a cue several times on a short, familiar walk.
gate.ownerCheck: On a familiar walk, does {dog} look back at you a few times without being asked?

stages.ifGateFails: Pick a quieter route, reward any glance your way, and use their name once if you need to.
stages.maintenance: Keep rewarding check-ins, especially in new places.

pathways.title: Settling calmly at home
pathways.summary: From relaxing on a mat to settling while ordinary home life goes on.

stages.title: Relaxing on a mat
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog goes to a mat or bed and relaxes there for a short time while you are nearby.
stages.whyItMatters: A place that means rest gives your dog somewhere to switch off, and you a way to help them calm down.
stages.everydayPractice: Quietly drop a treat on the mat whenever your dog chooses to lie there.

gate.summary: Lies down on the mat and stays relaxed for about a minute in a quiet room.
gate.ownerCheck: In a quiet room, does {dog} lie down on their mat and stay relaxed for about a minute?

stages.ifGateFails: Practise after a walk or play, when your dog is already tired, and reward calm more often.
stages.maintenance: Keep the mat a good place: reward calm there now and then.

stages.title: Settling while life goes on
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog settles while you do ordinary things at home, like cooking or watching TV.
stages.whyItMatters: Most of a dog's day is at home. Being able to rest while the house is busy helps them cope with everything else.
stages.everydayPractice: While you have a cup of tea, reward your dog for lying quietly nearby.

gate.summary: Settles for a few minutes while you do something ordinary in the same room.
gate.ownerCheck: While you get on with something ordinary at home, does {dog} settle for a few minutes?

stages.ifGateFails: Pick a quieter moment and a shorter time, and make sure your dog has had enough exercise and sleep. A dog who can't settle at all may be unwell or worried: speak to your vet.
stages.maintenance: Give your dog quiet rest times every day, and protect their sleep.

pathways.title: Greeting visitors calmly
pathways.summary: From four paws on the floor for a hello to waiting at the door when someone arrives.

stages.title: Four paws on the floor
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog keeps all four paws on the floor when someone they know says hello.
stages.whyItMatters: Jumping up is how many dogs say hello. Rewarding calm greetings shows them a better way that still gets attention.
stages.everydayPractice: When you come home, greet your dog only once all four paws are on the floor.

gate.summary: Keeps four paws on the floor while a familiar person says hello.
gate.ownerCheck: When someone {dog} knows says hello, do all four paws stay on the floor?

stages.ifGateFails: Ask people to greet more calmly and turn away if your dog jumps, and reward four paws on the floor straight away.
stages.maintenance: Everyone at home greets only calm paws on the floor.

stages.title: Waiting at the door
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog waits back from the door while it opens and a visitor comes in, until you say they can say hello.
stages.whyItMatters: The door is where greetings get exciting. Waiting there keeps everyone safe and gives your dog a calm start to the visit.
stages.everydayPractice: Before you open the door for a walk, wait for a calm moment, then open it as the reward.

gate.summary: Waits behind the door while it opens and a familiar visitor comes in, until released.
gate.ownerCheck: When a visitor {dog} knows comes in, does {dog} wait back from the door until you say they can say hello?

stages.ifGateFails: Practise the door with no one there first, or pop your dog behind a baby gate with something to chew while visitors arrive. If your dog seems worried rather than excited, give them space and get advice.
stages.maintenance: Keep the door calm: reward waiting, and use a gate on busy days.
